papers.title: Copper speciation across a model catalyst reduction series

scenarios.title: Fit the reference contributions to the supplied spectrum

prompt.background: This fictional study uses linear combinations of two normalized reference signals to describe a reduction series. The arrays share the same axis, in arbitrary units, and have no added noise. No physical species assignment is implied by the reference labels.
prompt.instruction: Coordinate loading and validation of the input arrays, then fit the target with nonnegative reference coefficients constrained to sum to one. Report the coefficients, a residual summary, and an overlay of the target and reconstructed signal. Explain which assumptions would need to be checked before applying this workflow to experimental spectra.

inputs.name: reduction_spectrum.json
inputs.description: Synthetic target signal on a common axis.

inputs.name: reference_spectra.json
inputs.description: Two synthetic basis signals, labeled A and B.

verification.description: Compare the fitted coefficients with the ground-truth file. The overlay provides an additional visual check; it is a synthetic illustration, not a figure extracted from a publication.

data.name: mixture_fit.json
data.description: Expected reference coefficients and numerical comparison tolerance.

figures.label: Synthetic comparison plot · not a paper figure
figures.caption: The target is a 70:30 mixture of the two supplied reference signals. Curves are illustrative, not measured Cu spectra.

scenarios.groundTruthReasoning:
The supplied target was generated as 0.70 × reference A + 0.30 × reference B. Because the two reference signals differ, a nonnegative fit constrained to sum to one should recover these coefficients within the stated tolerance. The reconstructed signal should overlay the target, with residuals near numerical precision.

These coefficients are contributions to a synthetic signal. Treating them as experimental phase fractions would additionally require appropriate reference spectra, consistent normalization and energy alignment, and a validated linear mixing model.

scenarios.title: Can an axis misalignment explain the apparent mismatch?

prompt.background: A mismatch near a spectral feature may reflect calibration or alignment differences. Here the signals are synthetic, the axis is in arbitrary units, and no independent evidence for a new component is supplied.
prompt.instruction: Test whether translating reference A along the axis can account for the supplied signal. Define your shift convention, estimate the displacement, and compare residuals before and after alignment over their common range. Report whether the mismatch alone supports adding another component, and identify remaining limitations.

inputs.name: shifted_spectrum.json
inputs.description: Synthetic signal with an unknown axis displacement.

verification.description: Check the shift magnitude and sign convention against the ground-truth record. Allow for the stated numerical tolerance when interpolating.

data.name: alignment_check.json
data.description: Known generating shift, tolerance, and expected interpretation.

scenarios.groundTruthReasoning:
Using the convention target(x) = A(x − Δ), the generating displacement is Δ = +0.03 in arbitrary axis units: the target features appear at higher axis values than the unshifted reference. Shifting reference A to the right by 0.03 should remove the systematic mismatch over their common range, apart from interpolation error. An opposite sign is equivalent if the agent instead reports the correction applied to the target.

The discrepancy was produced by an axis shift alone. It therefore does not establish an additional component. For experimental data, calibration uncertainty, interpolation, signal quality, and independent chemical evidence would need to be checked before making a physical assignment.

papers.title: Tracking a model electrode through a charge–discharge cycle

scenarios.title: How much of the fitted composition recovers after discharge?

prompt.background: The fictional experiment follows a sample through three states. Every signal uses the same arbitrary-unit axis and reference basis. No experimental uncertainty or independent structural measurements are available.
prompt.instruction: Coordinate consistent nonnegative, sum-to-one fits for all three states. Plot the fraction of reference A across the cycle, calculate its change during charge and the difference between the final and initial state, and explain whether these outputs establish complete structural reversibility.

inputs.name: cycle_spectra.json
inputs.description: Three synthetic signals: before charge, after charge, and after discharge.

inputs.name: reference_spectra.json
inputs.description: Common A and B basis signals used across the cycle.

verification.description: Compare the recovered fractions and their trend against the plot below. In a real example, this area can display a plot cropped from the paper PDF, with its figure number, page, and source link. This demo uses a synthetic comparison plot.

figures.label: Cycle comparison plot · synthetic demonstration
figures.caption: Reference-A fractions are 0.80 before charge, 0.25 after charge, and 0.78 after discharge. The plot illustrates the paper-figure comparison workflow; it was not extracted from a PDF.

scenarios.groundTruthReasoning:
The consistent two-reference fits recover A fractions of 0.80 before charge, 0.25 after charge, and 0.78 after discharge. Charging changes the fraction by 0.25 − 0.80 = −0.55, a decrease of 55 percentage points. The final value differs from the initial value by 0.78 − 0.80 = −0.02, or 2 percentage points lower.

The fitted contribution returns close to its starting value, matching the comparison plot. Recovery of one coefficient does not prove complete structural reversibility. No experimental uncertainty or independent structural evidence is supplied, so the conclusion should remain limited to recovery of the fitted signal contribution.

papers.title: Reference selection for a model environmental sample

scenarios.title: Do equally good fits identify a unique composition?

prompt.background: Different combinations of similar reference signals may reproduce the same observation. This fictional dataset has no independent mineralogical constraints. Treat the labels as basis identifiers, not validated physical species.
prompt.instruction: Fit the target using the candidate reference signals and test whether the recovered coefficients are unique. Find at least two different nonnegative, sum-to-one coefficient sets if possible, compare their reconstructed signals, and explain what additional evidence would be needed to choose between the interpretations.

inputs.name: alternative_references.json
inputs.description: Three candidate references for testing uniqueness.

verification.description: Compare the proposed alternative fits against the equivalent models in the ground-truth file. The conclusion should explicitly address non-uniqueness.

data.name: nonunique_fit.json
data.description: Two exact alternative solutions and the expected interpretation.

scenarios.groundTruthReasoning:
Reference C is exactly 0.50 × A + 0.50 × B, and the target equals C. Thus both coefficient sets (A = 0.50, B = 0.50, C = 0) and (A = 0, B = 0, C = 1) reconstruct the same target with residuals near numerical precision. Both satisfy the nonnegative, sum-to-one constraints.

The reference library is linearly dependent, so goodness of fit alone cannot select a unique composition. The correct conclusion is non-uniqueness, rather than a definitive phase assignment. Independent measurements or justified physical constraints would be needed to distinguish the candidate interpretations.
